<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q1: How many rows?</div>
<p class="quiz-question">You have survey data <code>survey</code> with one row per respondent:</p>

| respondent | country | trust |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Netherlands | 6 |
| 2 | Belgium | 4 |
| 3 | Netherlands | 7 |
| 4 | Luxembourg | 5 |

<p>And country-level data <code>countries</code> with GDP per capita (in thousands of dollars):

| country | gdp_pc |
|---|---:|
| Netherlands | 57 |
| Belgium | 50 |
| Germany | 48 |

<p>How many rows does <code>inner_join(survey, countries, join_by(country))</code> have?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — inner_join keeps every combination of rows that share a key value. Respondents 1 and 3 both match the Netherlands row, and respondent 2 matches Belgium, so the Netherlands GDP is simply repeated for both Dutch respondents (a one-to-many join). Luxembourg (no GDP data) and Germany (no respondents) are dropped.">3</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — a join doesn't produce one row per matching country; it produces one row per matching combination of rows. Both Dutch respondents match the Netherlands row, so each gets their own row in the result.">2</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — that's what left_join(survey, countries) would give: all four respondents, with NA for Luxembourg's GDP. inner_join drops rows that have no match in the other data set.">4</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — that's what full_join would give: all respondents plus an extra row for Germany (which has no respondents). inner_join keeps only rows with a match in both data sets.">5</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q2: Keeping all respondents</div>
<p class="quiz-question">Using the same <code>survey</code> and <code>countries</code> data as in Q1, you want to add GDP information to your respondents. Your analysis is about the respondents, so you want to keep all respondents, even the one from Luxembourg for which you have no GDP data. Which call do you use?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — left_join keeps all rows from the first (left) data set, here survey, and adds the columns of countries where there is a match. Respondent 4 gets NA for gdp_pc, and Germany (which has no respondents) is not added."><code>left_join(survey, countries, join_by(country))</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — inner_join only keeps rows with a match in both data sets, so the Luxembourg respondent would be silently dropped."><code>inner_join(survey, countries, join_by(country))</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — right_join keeps all rows of the second (right) data set, here countries. The Luxembourg respondent is dropped, and you get an extra row for Germany with NA for respondent and trust."><code>right_join(survey, countries, join_by(country))</code></li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — full_join does keep the Luxembourg respondent, but it also adds a row for Germany without any respondent. That row doesn't belong in a data set of respondents, so left_join is the better choice."><code>full_join(survey, countries, join_by(country))</code></li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q3: Two year columns</div>
<p class="quiz-question">You join CO2 data with World Bank income groups, both filtered to 2020:</p>

| country | year | co2 |
|---|---:|---:|
| India | 2020 | 2423 |
| Kenya | 2020 | 20 |

| country | year | income_group |
|---|---:|---|
| India | 2020 | Lower-middle-income |
| Kenya | 2020 | Lower-middle-income |

<p>The result of <code>inner_join(co2_2020, income_2020, join_by(country))</code> has columns <code>country</code>, <code>year.x</code>, <code>co2</code>, <code>year.y</code> and <code>income_group</code>. Why are there two year columns?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — only country is used as key. year is a non-key column that occurs in both data sets, and a data frame can't have two columns with the same name, so dplyr keeps both and adds the suffixes .x (left) and .y (right). Joining on join_by(country, year), or dropping year from one data set with select(), avoids this.">Because <code>year</code> exists in both data sets but is not one of the key columns, so both versions are kept and given a suffix.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — the year values are identical here (both 2020). dplyr doesn't look at the values: any non-key column that has the same name in both data sets gets a suffix.">Because the year values in the two data sets are different, so dplyr can't merge them into one column.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — each country occurs only once in each data set here, so this is a one-to-one join. The suffixes are about column names, not about the number of matching rows.">Because this is a many-to-many join, which always duplicates the columns.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — inner_join keeps rows that occur in both data sets, but the columns of both data sets are always all kept; this is not specific to inner_join.">Because <code>inner_join</code> keeps all columns from both data sets, while <code>left_join</code> would only keep the columns of the left data set.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q4: Joining panel waves</div>
<p class="quiz-question">You have two data frames from a panel survey, both with two waves for the same respondent:</p>

| respondent | wave | trust |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 6 |
| 1 | 2 | 4 |

| respondent | wave | income |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 2500 |
| 1 | 2 | 2700 |

<p>You run <code>inner_join(trust, income, join_by(respondent))</code>. What happens?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — since the join is only on respondent, each of the two trust rows matches both income rows, giving every combination: wave 1 trust with wave 2 income, and so on. dplyr warns about the unexpected many-to-many relationship. Since a row is really identified by respondent and wave, the fix is join_by(respondent, wave).">You get 4 rows, combining each trust wave with each income wave, and a warning about a many-to-many relationship; you should use <code>join_by(respondent, wave)</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — that would be the result of join_by(respondent, wave). A join doesn't look at columns that are not in join_by to decide which rows belong together; it only uses the key columns.">You get 2 rows, one per wave, because dplyr sees that the wave values match.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — a join never merges several rows into one. Each combination of matching rows becomes its own row.">You get 1 row for respondent 1, with the trust and income values of both waves combined.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — dplyr doesn't refuse the join; it performs it and gives a warning. You can silence the warning with relationship='many-to-many' if you really intended this, but here you probably didn't.">You get an error, because dplyr refuses to join data sets in which a key value occurs more than once.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>

<div class="quiz">
<div class="quiz-title">Q5: Finding what's missing</div>
<p class="quiz-question">After joining your CO2 and income data, the United States is missing from the result. You suspect the country is spelled differently in the two data sets:</p>

| country | co2 |
|---|---:|
| Netherlands | 137 |
| United States | 4690 |

| country | income_group |
|---|---|
| Netherlands | High-income |
| USA | High-income |

<p>What does <code>anti_join(co2_2020, income_2020, join_by(country))</code> return?</p>
<ul class="quiz-choices">
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="true" data-explain="Right — anti_join keeps the rows of the first data set that have no match in the second. 'United States' does not occur in income_2020, so that row is returned, with only the columns of co2_2020. This quickly shows which rows an inner_join would silently drop.">The <code>United States</code> row from <code>co2_2020</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — that would be anti_join(income_2020, co2_2020, ...), with the data sets the other way around. anti_join only returns rows from the first data set.">The <code>USA</code> row from <code>income_2020</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — that's what semi_join would return: the rows of the first data set that do have a match. anti_join is its opposite.">The <code>Netherlands</code> row from <code>co2_2020</code>.</li>
<li class="quiz-choice" data-correct="false" data-explain="Not quite — anti_join (like semi_join) only filters the rows of the first data set; it never adds columns or rows from the second data set.">Both the <code>United States</code> and the <code>USA</code> rows, with <code>NA</code> for the missing columns.</li>
</ul>
<p class="quiz-feedback" hidden></p>
</div>
